content:
Dev Patel: got a prospect email back w/ concern about “new throttling” they saw mentioned in a roadmap call. they’re asking what exactly changes + how they should handle 429s. also: when do we escalate for exceptions vs just “implement backoff”? looking for a crisp support answer we can reuse.

Owen Phillips: yep seeing this come up. we need consistent language: it’s not random throttling, it’s tier-aware protection to keep enterprise routes stable under fleet pressure.

Dev Patel: can someone give me customer-friendly phrasing + escalation criteria? (they’re evaluating Hosted API now, maybe Dedicated later)

Markus Klein: for prospects I’ve been saying:
- we added “capacity protection” to prevent noisy-neighbor overload from causing fleetwide latency/5xx
- under load, best-effort traffic gets throttled earlier/more predictably so higher-SLA traffic stays within SLO
- 429s include reason codes so you can tell quota vs transient overload

Simran Kaur: + emphasize determinism. customers hate “it depends”. We can say:
1) if you exceed contractual/plan rate limits or quotas → 429 (quota)
2) if the system is under regional pressure → we may return 429 even if you’re under nominal limits (overload protection)
Both should be retried with exponential backoff + jitter.

Nikhil Sharma: product framing: call it “hot-route capacity protection”. It’s there to keep `/v1/chat/completions`, embeddings, rerank stable for enterprise during spikes. We’re also making 429 semantics consistent.

Dev Patel: what do we tell them to do client-side? they asked “should we retry immediately”

Wei Chen: docs guidance (draft) is basically:
- honor `Retry-After` if present
- otherwise exponential backoff w/ jitter starting 250–500ms
- cap retries (e.g., 3–5) + fail fast w/ user-visible message if interactive
- do not retry streaming requests by reusing the same connection; open a new request

Owen Phillips: also: if they’re getting 429s, ask them to log the response headers. The new ones we’re standardizing on are:
- `x-redwood-429-reason`: `quota_exceeded` | `rate_limited` | `overload_protection` | `admission_control`
- `x-redwood-limit-scope`: `account` | `route` | `org`
- `x-request-id` for correlation
Then we can quickly tell whether it’s config vs fleet pressure.

Rachel Kim: + for enterprise conversations, reassure: if they are on an enterprise tier / have an SLA, they get priority budgets for protected routes. We don’t promise “no 429 ever”, but we do promise more predictable behavior and we’re protecting their latency/availability during bursts.

Dev Patel: ok but Support needs a hard line: when do we escalate for exceptions?

Markus Klein: proposed escalation triggers (what I use with Solutions):
- they are (or will be) on Enterprise / Dedicated AND they show sustained 429s impacting a production use case
- they have a time-bound launch event w/ known burst requirements (marketing, migration, etc.)
- their workload is “spiky but legitimate” and they can provide expected QPS + token/seq length distribution
- they can commit to implementing backoff + optionally a queue on their side
Non-escalation: “we got some 429s during testing”, “we want infinite burst”, “no retry/backoff implemented”.

Owen Phillips: + if reason is `quota_exceeded` or `rate_limited`, don’t escalate first—confirm their current limits + advise request shaping. escalate only if limit is wrong vs contract or docs.
If reason is `overload_protection` and they’re enterprise + it’s impacting a protected route for >10-15 min → escalate to on-call/SRE w/ request-id samples.

Nikhil Sharma: exception policy: we can do temporary burst exceptions, but they must be guarded (allowlist + cap + expiry). approval: Product (me) + SRE lead during rollout windows. We should not do “silent unlimited” overrides.

Wei Chen: I can drop a macro-ish blurb here. Feel free to reuse:
“Redwood returns HTTP 429 when you exceed configured rate/usage limits, or when the platform is under transient capacity pressure. As part of our capacity protection work, 429 behavior is now more consistent and includes headers that indicate why the request was rejected. Recommended handling is to honor `Retry-After` (if present) or use exponential backoff with jitter. If you’re seeing sustained 429s on a production workload, share 5–10 `x-request-id`s + the `x-redwood-429-reason` header and we’ll investigate and, if appropriate, review a temporary burst exception.”

Elliot Price: + link for internal use: Confluence known-issues doc “enterprise priority 429 + quota behavior” (support-facing) has the table of reason codes + what to say. I’ll make sure it includes this macro and the escalation checklist.

Dev Patel: perfect. last Q: prospect asked “does this mean you’ll downgrade model quality under load?”

Nikhil Sharma: answer: generally no. For enterprise protected routes, default behavior is admission control (throttle/shed) not silent fallback. Some routes may have explicitly-configured fallback to compatible variants/regions, but only where allowed + documented. We avoid silent quality changes.

Markus Klein: + if they want fallback for availability, that’s a solutions convo (explicit opt-in) not a surprise behavior.

Owen Phillips: :thumbsup: If you paste the prospect email + what tier they’re on, I can sanity check the response before it goes out.

Dev Patel: awesome, will reply w/ the macro + ask for headers + backoff confirmation. I’ll flag you if they push for exceptions. thanks all.
